STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, real problem: cost-driven medication non-adherence among young adults with chronic conditions is well documented, with a credible downstream cost story (ER visits). (2) Sensible product scope: price comparison + program matching + budgeting/refill reminders is a coherent bundle, and the plain-language/education angle fits an inexperienced user base. (3) Honest, self-aware plan: founders openly flag unsigned referral deals, unproven conversion, unrefined market size, and regulatory/privacy gaps, which signals coachability and low risk of overstated claims. (4) Capital-efficient execution so far: working prototype, first outside users, Delaware C-corp formed, only a few thousand dollars spent. (5) Complementary student team (public health/product, CS/build, business/partnerships) with a practical beachhead (campus health centers, student groups) and a focused 12-month goal (prove savings and retention) that sets up a logical next raise. (6) Free core product aligned with the target users' limited ability to pay.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Weak differentiation in a crowded, commoditized category: GoodRx-type services, pharmacy and insurer apps, and online generics players have data, brand, and distribution; budgeting and young-adult focus are easy for incumbents to copy and are not defensible moats. (2) Fragile monetization: referral revenue depends on unsigned agreements, and the target segment is low-spend with few prescriptions, so revenue per user is likely tiny; subscription willingness to pay among cost-constrained users is doubtful and contradicts the premise. Unit economics, CAC, and LTV are absent. (3) Data dependency: accurate, current pharmacy cash-price data is licensed, costly, and typically controlled by the very players who compete; the prototype uses limited public/sample data, so core value is unproven at real-world accuracy. (4) Traction is thin: a small pilot with no measured savings, retention, or engagement; no evidence users will change behavior or that savings are meaningful versus existing tools. (5) Market sizing is vague ('several million,' unrefined), and secondary markets are untested. (6) Regulatory and privacy exposure is substantial and unaddressed: handling health-related data (HIPAA adjacency, state privacy laws), coupon and anti-kickback considerations with referral fees, and no compliance plan or expertise on the team. (7) Team limitations: students with no healthcare industry, pharmacy-benefit, or partnership experience; advisors are informal; competing academic commitments raise full-time-commitment risk. (8) Distribution plan is campus-local and may not scale; no clear low-cost acquisition channel beyond university contacts. (9) No financial model; the $75K ask is loosely justified.

OVERALL: Meaningful problem and a candid, capable early team, but a crowded market, unvalidated differentiation and monetization, data and regulatory hurdles, and minimal traction make this a high-risk, pre-seed idea. Investment interest is low-to-moderate: appropriate for small competition or grant-style funding and mentorship to test hypotheses, not yet for institutional venture investment until retention, measured savings, and at least one signed referral or data partner are demonstrated.
